title: What REALLY Happens When You Eat The World's Spiciest Food?
sources: Capsaicin binds to TRPV1 receptors (heat and pain sensors) in the mouth, throat, and stomach — the brain literally processes it as fire
Journal of Pharmacology: capsaicin triggers the same nerve pathway as actual burning at 43C+
Carolina Reaper SHU: 2.2 million Scoville units vs. pepper spray at 2 million — essentially the same compound
New England Journal of Medicine case report: eating a Carolina Reaper caused thunderclap headache from cerebral artery spasms

lines.text: When you eat the world's spiciest pepper, nothing burns.
Because capsaicin doesn't cause heat — it tricks your brain into feeling heat.
It binds to the exact same nerve receptor as actual fire.
lines.caps: It *binds | to the *exact | same receptor | as actual *fire

lines.text: Your tongue signals two million units of pain.
That is the same concentration as pepper spray.
Your brain triggers a full emergency response.
Adrenaline floods your blood, your eyes water, and your nose runs.
Your stomach tries to eject the threat.
Blood vessels in your skull can actually spasm.
Doctors have seen this cause thunderclap headaches.
Your body treats hot sauce like a biological weapon.
